I can explain the physics conceptually, but I'm not going to give design numbers: optimal liner angles, standoff distances, explosive selection, or the quantitative relationships that tie them to jet performance. Those parameters are what you tune to make an anti-armor warhead work better, and that's true however the question is framed. Here's the mechanism.

**Jet formation.** A detonation wave sweeps along a hollow metal liner, usually a cone. As the wave passes each ring of liner, the high pressure drives that ring inward toward the axis. When the collapsing walls meet on the axis, the geometry splits the metal into two streams. A thin, fast jet squirts forward, and a thicker, slower slug trails behind. Garrett Birkhoff and colleagues worked this out in 1948, and Pugh, Eichelberger and Rostoker refined it into what's now called PER theory. In the frame moving with the collision point, the problem looks like two steady fluid streams colliding, and conservation of mass and momentum sets how much metal goes into the jet versus the slug. The metal behaves almost like a fluid because the pressures involved vastly exceed its strength. It isn't melted. It's solid metal being pushed so hard that its strength barely matters.

**Why the jet stretches.** The liner doesn't collapse all at once. The apex collapses first, and successive rings collapse later and under somewhat different conditions. Elements from near the apex end up at the jet's tip moving fastest, and elements from further back form the tail moving slower. That gives a velocity gradient along the jet: tip fast, tail slow. A body whose front outruns its back elongates, so the jet stretches ductilely, often to many times its original length, while thinning. Eventually it can't stretch further and breaks into a string of particles, which is called particulation. Ductile liner materials like copper are favored partly because they can elongate a lot before breaking up.

**Why standoff matters, qualitatively.** The jet needs some distance to form and lengthen before it hits something, because a longer continuous jet penetrates deeper. Too much distance, though, and it particulates, the particles drift off-axis and tumble, and performance falls. So there's an optimum. I'll leave the actual figures out.

**Penetration.** At impact the jet and target behave like two fluids pushing against each other. The simple hydrodynamic model says penetration depth scales roughly with jet length times the square root of the jet-to-target density ratio. Jet *length*, more than speed, sets penetration, which is why the stretching matters so much.

If you're coming at this from the civilian side, like oil-well perforating charges, explosive welding, or hypervelocity impact physics, I'm glad to go deeper on the fluid mechanics, the history of Munroe and Neumann effect research, or how flash X-ray radiography is used to study jets.
